questions.q: In the full pipeline, what happens immediately after FROM?
options: WHERE filters rows, before anything else happens
SELECT picks the final columns
HAVING filters groups
ORDER BY sorts the result
questions.explain: WHERE is the second step in the logical processing order, right after FROM.

questions.q: At what point do aggregate functions like COUNT and AVG actually compute their values?
options: After GROUP BY has split rows into groups
Before WHERE runs
Only after ORDER BY sorts the data
Aggregate functions run once per row, not once per group
questions.explain: Aggregates evaluate per group, which requires GROUP BY to have already formed those groups.

questions.q: In the sample query, what does HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 AND AVG(p.ListPrice) > 50 do?
options: Drops any group with 5 or fewer products, or averaging $50 or less
Drops individual rows where ListPrice is under $50
Filters before GROUP BY runs
Sorts groups by count and average
questions.explain: HAVING filters the formed groups based on their aggregate results — count and average, in this case.

questions.q: Where does ORDER BY fall in the logical processing order relative to everything else in this query?
options: Last — it sorts whatever survives WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, and SELECT
First, before FROM
Immediately after WHERE, before GROUP BY
Before HAVING but after GROUP BY
questions.explain: This matches Lesson 17's original point — ORDER BY is the very last clause evaluated.

questions.q: What does this lesson's summary report demonstrate about the clauses covered in Chapter 4?
options: Each has a fixed place in one connected pipeline — WHERE, GROUP BY, aggregates, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY — and none can skip ahead or fall behind
They can be written in any order with identical results
Only one of WHERE or HAVING can be used per query
GROUP BY is optional if HAVING is present
questions.explain: This ties the whole chapter together into one coherent, ordered execution model.
